rounds.title: Real or fake?
rounds.intro: Six headlines about AI in UK politics. Some happened. Some didn't. Trust your radar.

rounds.title: How AI works
rounds.intro: How chatbots write their answers, and how AI tells politicians how many people like them.

rounds.title: Campaigns are marketing
rounds.intro: Parties are brands and voters are customers. How well do you know the AI marketing toolkit?

rounds.title: Fakes, facts & rules
rounds.intro: Deepfakes, chatbots that get it wrong, and the law that's still being written.

questions.question: “An AI candidate stood for Parliament in the 2024 general election.”
questions.explanation: Real: ‘AI Steve’ stood in Brighton Pavilion, with a human candidate behind the avatar.

questions.question: “MPs can now send an AI avatar to vote for them in Parliament.”
questions.explanation: Fake: only elected MPs can vote in the Commons, never an AI avatar.

questions.question: “A cabinet minister asked ChatGPT which podcasts he should go on.”
questions.explanation: Real: a Freedom of Information request revealed Tech Secretary Peter Kyle’s ChatGPT chats.

questions.question: “The UK banned all AI-made political adverts in 2026.”
questions.explanation: Fake: there’s no ban, only guidance that AI content is labelled and not misleading.

questions.question: “Scammers paid for deepfake Facebook adverts using Rishi Sunak’s face while he was Prime Minister.”
questions.explanation: Real: 143 deepfake scam ads of Sunak reached up to 400,000 people in 2024.
questions.source_name: Fenimore Harper research, via Engadget, Jan 2024

questions.question: “Researchers found that AI fakes changed the result of the 2024 general election.”
questions.explanation: Fake: the Alan Turing Institute found no evidence AI fakes changed the 2024 result.

questions.question: How does a chatbot like ChatGPT write its answers?
options: It looks each fact up in a database
It predicts the next most likely word
questions.answer: It predicts the next most likely word
questions.explanation: Chatbots predict the next likely word, so answers can sound right but be wrong.
questions.source_name: GOV.UK, AI Playbook for the UK Government, Feb 2025

questions.question: YouGov’s final MRP poll before the 2024 general election said Labour would win 431 seats. How many did Labour actually win?
questions.explanation: 411: the MRP overshot Labour by 20 seats but nailed the Lib Dems.
questions.source_name: YouGov, 3 July 2024; UK Parliament election results

questions.question: Ipsos used AI ‘social listening’ on 950,000+ posts during the 2024 election campaign. What did it find?
options: Most posts about party leaders were positive
Talk about every party leader was more negative than positive
questions.answer: Talk about every party leader was more negative than positive
questions.explanation: Mostly negative: talk about every leader leaned negative, but loud posters aren’t the whole country.

questions.question: ‘AI Steve’ stood in Brighton Pavilion in 2024, promising voters 24/7 access through his AI avatar. How many votes did he get?
questions.explanation: 179: ‘AI Steve’ got just 0.3% of the vote, last of 8 candidates.

questions.question: AI Steve got coverage from The Guardian to NBC News, but only 179 votes. What’s the marketing lesson?
options: Attention isn’t the same as trust
questions.answer: Attention isn’t the same as trust
questions.explanation: Attention isn’t trust: the campaign won worldwide publicity, but not votes.

questions.question: In the six weeks of the 2024 general election, how much did parties and campaigners spend on Facebook, Instagram and Google ads?
Ad platforms help parties find ‘lookalike audiences’. What are they?
options: People who resemble a party’s existing supporters
Actors who look like the party leader
Fake accounts that copy real voters
Voters who live on the same street
questions.answer: People who resemble a party’s existing supporters
questions.explanation: People like a party’s supporters; about 1 in 5 early 2024 Meta ads used them.

questions.question: The government’s AI tool ‘Consult’ sorted 50,000+ public responses about the water industry. How long did it take?
questions.explanation: About 2 hours, matching human experts and potentially saving 75,000 days of work a year.

questions.question: Before Scotland’s May 2026 election, researchers asked AI chatbots questions about the election. How many of the answers contained factual errors?
questions.explanation: More than 1 in 3: ChatGPT got the election date wrong by over two months.

questions.question: Before the May 2026 local elections, what share of voters said they’d seen a deepfake or AI-made content about a candidate?
questions.explanation: 30%: almost one in three voters, in a Demos poll of 2,000+ people.

questions.question: In October 2023, fake audio of Keir Starmer (then Labour leader) swearing at staff spread on X. Roughly how many views did it get?
questions.explanation: 1.5 million views, and X refused to take the fake audio down.

questions.question: AI can fight fake AI too. Roughly how many social media posts did the Electoral Commission’s AI scan for deepfakes during the May 2026 elections?
questions.explanation: 3 million posts: 147 flagged for humans, 10 sent to platforms or police.

questions.question: Which of these is already an election offence in the UK?
options: Using AI to write campaign slogans
Making a false statement of fact about a candidate’s personal character or conduct
Posting an AI image that’s clearly labelled as AI
questions.answer: Making a false statement of fact about a candidate’s personal character or conduct
questions.explanation: False statements about a candidate’s character are illegal; whether deepfakes count is still unclear.
questions.source_name: Full Fact briefing on political deepfakes, 2026
